title: Configure WLAN components for client connectivity

questions.question: What is the maximum length of an SSID?
questions.explanation: An SSID can be up to 32 characters.

correct.explanation: An SSID name can be up to 32 characters — the IEEE 802.11 standard limit for the SSID field.

incorrect.explanation: 16 characters is below the maximum — 802.11 allows SSIDs up to 32 characters.
incorrect.whatItDoes: 16 characters points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for An SSID can be up to 32 characters.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "An SSID can be up to 32 characters", 32 characters satisfies what this question tests — 16 characters does not.

incorrect.explanation: 48 characters exceeds the 802.11 SSID field — maximum is 32 characters.
incorrect.whatItDoes: 48 characters points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for An SSID can be up to 32 characters.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "An SSID can be up to 32 characters", 32 characters satisfies what this question tests — 48 characters does not.

incorrect.explanation: 64 characters is double the allowed SSID length — memorize 32 for CCNA.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Confusing SSID limit with 64-bit WPA key
incorrect.whatItDoes: 64 characters points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for An SSID can be up to 32 characters.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "An SSID can be up to 32 characters", 32 characters satisfies what this question tests — 64 characters does not.

answerReview.examTip: SSID max length = 32 characters (802.11); WPA2-PSK passphrase is separate.

questions.question: You are running a WLC for a WLAN. You want to allow for guests to be segmented to the guest VLAN. What is the simplest implementation you can configure on the WLC?
choices: Access control lists for one SSID
Two SSIDs, one configured to the production VLAN and another configured to the guest VLAN
Access control lists for two SSIDs
questions.explanation: A simple guest segmentation design uses separate SSIDs mapped to production and guest VLANs.

correct.explanation: Simplest segmentation: two SSIDs — one mapped to production VLAN, one to guest VLAN. Clients associate to the appropriate SSID.

incorrect.explanation: One SSID with ACLs does not provide VLAN segmentation — traffic stays on same VLAN.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Access control lists for one SSID points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for segmented.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "segmented", Two SSIDs, one configured to the production VLAN and another configured to the guest VLAN satisfies what this question tests — Access control lists for one SSID does not.

incorrect.explanation: Dynamic VLANs (RADIUS-assigned) work but are more complex than simply creating two SSIDs.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Dynamic VLANs for the SSID points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for segmented.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "segmented", Two SSIDs, one configured to the production VLAN and another configured to the guest VLAN satisfies what this question tests — Dynamic VLANs for the SSID does not.

incorrect.explanation: Two SSIDs with ACLs is overkill when VLAN assignment per SSID achieves the goal simply.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: ACLs on both SSIDs for segmentation
incorrect.whatItDoes: Access control lists for two SSIDs points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for segmented.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "segmented", Two SSIDs, one configured to the production VLAN and another configured to the guest VLAN satisfies what this question tests — Access control lists for two SSIDs does not.

answerReview.examTip: Guest segmentation on WLC: separate SSID → mapped to guest VLAN — simple and effective.

questions.question: You company has been contracted to implement a 802.11 wireless system for a small town. Which type of implementation is this considered?
questions.explanation: A town-wide wireless deployment is a WMAN.

correct.explanation: A wireless system covering a town is a WMAN (Wireless Metropolitan Area Network).

incorrect.explanation: WPAN = personal area (Bluetooth, ~10m) — a town is much larger.
incorrect.whatItDoes: WPAN points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for A town-wide wireless deployment is a WMAN.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "A town-wide wireless deployment is a WMAN", WMAN satisfies what this question tests — WPAN does not.

incorrect.explanation: WLAN = local (building/campus) — a town exceeds LAN scale.
incorrect.whatItDoes: WLAN points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for A town-wide wireless deployment is a WMAN.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "A town-wide wireless deployment is a WMAN", WMAN satisfies what this question tests — WLAN does not.

incorrect.explanation: WWAN = wide area (cellular, country-scale) — a single town is metropolitan.
incorrect.whatItDoes: WWAN points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for A town-wide wireless deployment is a WMAN.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "A town-wide wireless deployment is a WMAN", WMAN satisfies what this question tests — WWAN does not.

answerReview.examTip: WPAN < WLAN < WMAN < WWAN — town/city = MAN (Metropolitan).

questions.question: What is the term for a small wireless network that does not extend past 30 feet?
questions.explanation: A short-range personal wireless network is a WPAN.

correct.explanation: WPAN (Wireless Personal Area Network) covers short range (~10–30 feet) — Bluetooth and similar personal devices.

incorrect.explanation: WLAN is a local area wireless network (building/campus scale) — not a 30-foot personal bubble.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Labeling short-range personal network as WLAN
incorrect.whatItDoes: WLAN points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for A short-range personal wireless network is a WPAN.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "A short-range personal wireless network is a WPAN", WPAN satisfies what this question tests — WLAN does not.

incorrect.explanation: WMAN is metropolitan-scale wireless (city coverage) — far larger than 30 feet.
incorrect.whatItDoes: WMAN points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for A short-range personal wireless network is a WPAN.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "A short-range personal wireless network is a WPAN", WPAN satisfies what this question tests — WMAN does not.

incorrect.explanation: WWAN is wide-area cellular/mobile — not a small personal wireless network.
incorrect.whatItDoes: WWAN points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for A short-range personal wireless network is a WPAN.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "A short-range personal wireless network is a WPAN", WPAN satisfies what this question tests — WWAN does not.

answerReview.examTip: Short personal range (~30 ft) → WPAN; building = WLAN; city = WMAN.

questions.question: What is the definition of a trust boundary in relation to QoS?
choices: A trust boundary is where the QoS markings are first configured.
A trust boundary is where the QoS markings are stripped at the router.
A trust boundary is where the network begins to trust the QoS markings from devices.
A trust boundary is the separation of QoS queues based upon their priority.
questions.explanation: A QoS trust boundary is where the network begins trusting QoS markings.

correct.explanation: A trust boundary is where the network begins trusting QoS markings from devices — beyond it, markings may be re-written.

incorrect.explanation: QoS markings are first applied at the device — the trust boundary is where the network accepts them.
incorrect.whatItDoes: A trust boundary is where the QoS markings are first configured. points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for A QoS trust boundary is where the network begins trusting QoS markings.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "A QoS trust boundary is where the network begins trusting QoS markings", A trust boundary is where the network begins to trust the QoS markings from devices. satisfies what this question tests — A trust boundary is where the QoS markings are first configured. does not.

incorrect.explanation: Stripping markings happens at untrusted boundaries — the trust boundary is where they're accepted.
incorrect.whatItDoes: A trust boundary is where the QoS markings are stripped at the router. applies another routing protocol's behavior instead of OSPF-specific rules.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "A QoS trust boundary is where the network begins trusting QoS markings", A trust boundary is where the network begins to trust the QoS markings from devices. satisfies what this question tests — A trust boundary is where the QoS markings are stripped at the router. does not.

incorrect.explanation: Queue separation is scheduling — the trust boundary is about marking acceptance.
incorrect.whatItDoes: A trust boundary is the separation of QoS queues based upon their priority. points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for A QoS trust boundary is where the network begins trusting QoS markings.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "A QoS trust boundary is where the network begins trusting QoS markings", A trust boundary is where the network begins to trust the QoS markings from devices. satisfies what this question tests — A trust boundary is the separation of QoS queues based upon their priority. does not.

answerReview.examTip: Trust boundary = point where network trusts device QoS markings (usually at the access switch).

questions.question: Which IEEE specification defines WLAN QoS for wireless data?

correct.explanation: 802.11e defines QoS enhancements for wireless LANs (WMM — Wi-Fi Multimedia).

incorrect.explanation: 802.11r is fast BSS transition (roaming) — not QoS.
incorrect.whatItDoes: 802.11r points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for specification.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "specification", 802.11e satisfies what this question tests — 802.11r does not.

incorrect.explanation: 802.1p is wired L2 CoS marking — not a wireless standard.
incorrect.whatItDoes: 802.1p points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for specification.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "specification", 802.11e satisfies what this question tests — 802.1p does not.

incorrect.explanation: 802.11k assists roaming decisions (neighbor reports) — not QoS.
incorrect.whatItDoes: 802.11k points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for specification.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "specification", 802.11e satisfies what this question tests — 802.11k does not.

answerReview.examTip: Wireless QoS = 802.11e (WMM) | Fast roaming = 802.11r | Neighbor list = 802.11k.

questions.question: You are creating a WLAN in the GUI of the WLC. You need to make sure that only corporate hosts can connect to the newly formed WLAN. How can you achieve this?
questions.explanation: MAC filtering can restrict WLAN access to known corporate hosts.

correct.explanation: MAC filtering allows only approved corporate MAC addresses to associate — restricts WLAN access to known devices.

incorrect.explanation: Disabling SSID broadcast hides the name — it does not authenticate or restrict which hosts can connect.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Using hidden SSID as corporate-only access control
incorrect.whatItDoes: Disable SSID broadcasting describes flooding the frame to multiple ports in the VLAN.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "MAC filtering can restrict WLAN access to known corporate hosts", Use MAC filtering satisfies what this question tests — Disable SSID broadcasting does not.

incorrect.explanation: A shared PSK lets anyone with the password connect — it does not limit to corporate-owned devices.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: PSK alone for corporate-only host restriction
incorrect.whatItDoes: Set a unique PSK points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for MAC filtering can restrict WLAN access to known corporate hosts.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "MAC filtering can restrict WLAN access to known corporate hosts", Use MAC filtering satisfies what this question tests — Set a unique PSK does not.

incorrect.explanation: LDAP enables user-based 802.1X authentication — the stem asks for corporate host restriction, which MAC filtering addresses directly.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Choosing LDAP when MAC allow-list is the simpler host filter
incorrect.whatItDoes: Add an LDAP server points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for MAC filtering can restrict WLAN access to known corporate hosts.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "MAC filtering can restrict WLAN access to known corporate hosts", Use MAC filtering satisfies what this question tests — Add an LDAP server does not.

answerReview.examTip: Corporate devices only → MAC filtering (or 802.1X with cert). PSK ≠ device allow-list.

questions.question: Which protocol should be enabled on a WLAN to allow a client device to download a list of neighboring WAPs?
questions.explanation: 802.11k lets clients learn neighboring AP information.

correct.explanation: 802.11k provides neighbor AP reports — clients use them to make faster roaming decisions.

incorrect.explanation: 802.11r is fast BSS transition (pre-auth key) — 802.11k provides the AP list.
incorrect.whatItDoes: 802.11r points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for protocol.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "protocol", 802.11k satisfies what this question tests — 802.11r does not.

incorrect.explanation: 802.11e is QoS (WMM) — not neighbor AP discovery.
incorrect.whatItDoes: 802.11e points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for protocol.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "protocol", 802.11k satisfies what this question tests — 802.11e does not.

incorrect.explanation: 802.11ac is a PHY speed standard (Wave 1/2) — not a roaming protocol.
incorrect.whatItDoes: 802.11ac points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for protocol.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "protocol", 802.11k satisfies what this question tests — 802.11ac does not.

answerReview.examTip: 802.11k = neighbor report (AP list) | 802.11r = fast roaming (pre-auth) | 802.11v = BSS transition mgmt.

questions.question: You are planning to implement wireless VoIP phones in your wireless network. Which QoS profile should you associate with the wireless network for the VoIP phones?
questions.explanation: Platinum is the WLC QoS profile appropriate for voice.

correct.explanation: VoIP needs the highest QoS priority — Platinum profile on Cisco WLC gives EF/voice treatment.

incorrect.explanation: Bronze is best-effort/background — not suitable for real-time voice.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Bronze points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for Platinum is the WLC QoS profile appropriate for voice.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "Platinum is the WLC QoS profile appropriate for voice", Platinum satisfies what this question tests — Bronze does not.

incorrect.explanation: Silver is standard data — voice requires Platinum for low latency.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Silver points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for Platinum is the WLC QoS profile appropriate for voice.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "Platinum is the WLC QoS profile appropriate for voice", Platinum satisfies what this question tests — Silver does not.

incorrect.explanation: Gold is video-grade — voice uses Platinum for the tightest latency/jitter.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Gold points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for Platinum is the WLC QoS profile appropriate for voice.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "Platinum is the WLC QoS profile appropriate for voice", Platinum satisfies what this question tests — Gold does not.

answerReview.examTip: WLC QoS profiles: Platinum (voice) > Gold (video) > Silver (best effort) > Bronze (background).

questions.question:
WLC WLAN summary — MaintDept:
Profile Name: MaintDept
Status: Disabled
Radio Policy: All
Multicast VLAN: Disabled
Broadcast SSID: Disabled

You were just notified by your maintenance department that they lost all wireless connectivity. Earlier you had a contractor working on the WLC. You log into the WLC and click on the WLAN of MaintDept shown below. What can you do to correct the problem?
questions.explanation: If a WLAN is disabled in the GUI, enabling status restores client access.

correct.explanation: WLAN status is Disabled — enable the WLAN so maintenance users can associate.

incorrect.explanation: Radio Policy "All" is correct — changing it won't fix a disabled WLAN.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Radio policy change for disabled WLAN
incorrect.whatItDoes: Change the radio policy points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for If a WLAN is disabled in the GUI, enabling status restores client access.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "If a WLAN is disabled in the GUI, enabling status restores client access", Enable the status satisfies what this question tests — Change the radio policy does not.

incorrect.explanation: Multicast VLAN is optional — the WLAN must be enabled first before any feature works.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Enable multicast VLAN to fix connectivity
incorrect.whatItDoes: Enable Multicast VLAN Feature gives a broadcast or multicast MAC pattern that may not be the all-ones form tested here.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: Ethernet addressing (If a WLAN is disabled in the GUI, enabling status restores client access): Enable the status is the broadcast/multicast form this stem expects — Enable Multicast VLAN Feature uses the wrong MAC pattern.

incorrect.explanation: Broadcast SSID being disabled hides the name but doesn't prevent connections — the WLAN being Disabled is the issue.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Enable Broadcast SSID describes flooding the frame to multiple ports in the VLAN.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "If a WLAN is disabled in the GUI, enabling status restores client access", Enable the status satisfies what this question tests — Enable Broadcast SSID does not.

answerReview.examTip: WLC WLAN not working → check Status first — must be Enabled for any client associations.

questions.question:
WLC WLAN security — CorpWLAN:
Security Policy: WPA2
Authentication Key Mgmt: PSK
Encryption: AES-CCMP (WPA2 Personal)

Which statement is true about the WLAN below?

correct.explanation: WPA2-PSK with AES (CCMP) is the shown profile — pre-shared key with AES encryption.

incorrect.explanation: WEP is obsolete — the profile explicitly shows WPA2 with AES, not WEP.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Choosing WEP when WPA2-AES is configured
incorrect.whatItDoes: WPA is enabled. points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for The WPA2 personal/PSK security.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "The WPA2 personal/PSK security", WPA2 personal is enabled. satisfies what this question tests — WPA is enabled. does not.

incorrect.explanation: WPA (TKIP) is older than WPA2 — the WLAN summary lists WPA2 security policy.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Downgrading WPA2 profile to original WPA
incorrect.whatItDoes: WPA2 enterprise is enabled. points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for The WPA2 personal/PSK security.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "The WPA2 personal/PSK security", WPA2 personal is enabled. satisfies what this question tests — WPA2 enterprise is enabled. does not.

incorrect.explanation: Open authentication has no PSK — this WLAN uses WPA2 with PSK key management.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Selecting open auth on a WPA2-PSK WLAN
incorrect.whatItDoes: 802.1X is enabled. points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for The WPA2 personal/PSK security.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "The WPA2 personal/PSK security", WPA2 personal is enabled. satisfies what this question tests — 802.1X is enabled. does not.

answerReview.examTip: WLC WLAN WPA2 + PSK + AES = WPA2-Personal (not WEP/Open).

questions.question: You need to set up a WLAN for connectivity to send and receive large files to roaming clients. The WLAN will exist with other WLAN traffic. Which QoS profile should the new WLAN be associated with?
questions.explanation: Bronze is the lowest QoS profile and is appropriate for low-priority bulk traffic in this source context.

correct.explanation: Large file transfer is bulk/background traffic — Bronze (best effort, no priority) is appropriate alongside other WLANs.

incorrect.explanation: Gold is video-tier — file transfers don't need low-latency treatment.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Gold profile for bulk file transfer
incorrect.whatItDoes: Gold points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for connectivity.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "connectivity", Bronze satisfies what this question tests — Gold does not.

incorrect.explanation: Platinum is voice — absolutely not for bulk file downloads.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Platinum points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for connectivity.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "connectivity", Bronze satisfies what this question tests — Platinum does not.

incorrect.explanation: Silver is standard data — but bulk/roaming file transfers should be Bronze to not compete with interactive traffic.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Silver for bulk file transfer WLAN
incorrect.whatItDoes: Silver points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for connectivity.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "connectivity", Bronze satisfies what this question tests — Silver does not.

answerReview.examTip: Large files/bulk = Bronze (background) | Interactive = Silver | Video = Gold | Voice = Platinum.

questions.question: Which type of security can be implemented on a WLAN that requires the host PC to present a certificate before being allowed onto the wireless network?
questions.explanation: 802.1X can require certificate-based authentication for WLAN access.

correct.explanation: 802.1X requires the client to present a certificate (or credentials via EAP) before network access — per-user authentication.

incorrect.explanation: MAC filtering checks hardware addresses — does not require certificates.
incorrect.whatItDoes: MAC filtering points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for security.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "security", 802.1X satisfies what this question tests — MAC filtering does not.

incorrect.explanation: WPA2 PSK uses a shared passphrase — no per-device certificates.
incorrect.whatItDoes: WPA2 PSK points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for security.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "security", 802.1X satisfies what this question tests — WPA2 PSK does not.

incorrect.explanation: Fast Transitioning (802.11r) speeds roaming — it's not a certificate-based admission control.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Fast Transitioning points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for security.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "security", 802.1X satisfies what this question tests — Fast Transitioning does not.

answerReview.examTip: Certificate-based WLAN access → 802.1X (EAP-TLS) — client and server exchange certificates via RADIUS.
